study type: Controlled observational study with a randomized intervention arm
exposure: Mode of delivery (vaginal vs. elective cesarean section)
Povidone-iodine perineal disinfection during vaginal delivery (conventional disinfection vs. non-disinfection)
outcome: Infant oral microflora composition (relative abundance of Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Lactobacillus, Prevotella, Escherichia-Shigella, Staphyloccus, Klebsiella)
KEGG pathways (e.g., staphylococcus aureus infection, viral myocarditis, sporulation)
cohort: The study included 30 full-term neonates (20 born vaginally, 10 by elective cesarean section) delivered in October 2017 at Shenzhen Bao'an Maternity and Child Health Hospital.
finding: Both mode of delivery and perineal disinfection during vaginal birth significantly affect the colonization of neonatal oral microbiota, with disinfection and cesarean section leading to similar microbial profiles characterized by lower Lactobacillus and higher relative abundances of potentially harmful bacteria.
mod_finding: The mode of delivery affects the infant's Lactobacillus acquisition from the mother, with infants born via cesarean section having extremely low Lactobacillus abundance, similar to vaginally born infants who underwent perineal disinfection.
